name: Minoxidil sublingual (SLM)

card.summary: A formulation of minoxidil placed under the tongue, being developed to regrow scalp hair with fewer side effects than swallowed minoxidil.
card.note: Still in clinical development; not an approved hair-loss product.

quick.overview:
Sublingual minoxidil (SLM) is minoxidil taken by dissolving it under the tongue instead of swallowing it. It is being developed for hair loss, aiming to keep the hair-regrowth effect of low-dose oral minoxidil while improving tolerability.

As described on Wikipedia, absorption under the tongue bypasses first-pass liver metabolism and peaks in about 30 minutes, and a preliminary trial of a low-dose version reported no adverse effects or blood pressure changes. A sublingual product from Samson Clinical was listed in phase 3 as of September 2025.
quick.how: In trials the drug is a small dissolving form placed under the tongue. Users of oral minoxidil for hair loss typically see changes over many months, and the sublingual form is aimed at the same type of pattern hair loss. Dosing and sourcing are matters for a prescribing clinician.
quick.risks: Oral minoxidil is associated with low blood pressure, fluid retention, rapid heartbeat, dizziness, headaches, excess hair growth and temporary shedding; rare serious cardiovascular events are reported mainly at higher doses. The sublingual form is investigational, and its safety profile is still being established.

lead: Sublingual minoxidil (SLM) is a formulation of minoxidil absorbed under the tongue, developed for hair loss [1]. Low-dose oral minoxidil is already used off-label to regrow hair, and SLM is intended to retain similar effectiveness while being better tolerated [1].

Absorption through the lining of the mouth bypasses first-pass metabolism in the liver, and peak blood levels are reached in about 30 minutes [1]. In a preliminary trial, a low-dose sublingual product caused no adverse effects or blood pressure changes [1].

As of September 2025, a sublingual minoxidil product developed by Samson Clinical was reported in phase 3 trials for hair loss, with its pharmacokinetics also under study [1]. Appearance benefits, therefore, are the potential regrowth of thinning scalp hair rather than an established outcome.

chain: Stimulates hair follicles in pattern hair loss
Thicker, fuller scalp hair over months
angle.text: Minoxidil is used to thicken thinning hair, and SLM is a route of delivery aimed at the same goal with a different tolerability profile. People interested in it are generally those who want oral-type minoxidil without some of its side effects.

infobox: Upjohn, early 1960s; oral tablets FDA-approved for hypertension 1979

paras: Minoxidil was developed by Upjohn in the early 1960s and introduced for high blood pressure in the 1970s, with oral tablets approved by the FDA in 1979 [1]. Hair growth was noticed as a side effect, leading to topical minoxidil approval for male baldness in 1988 as Rogaine, a women's version in 1991 and over-the-counter sales in 1996 [1]. Low-dose oral use for hair loss emerged around 2015 and grew in popularity after a 2022 media report [1].

Wikipedia describes SLM as potentially better tolerated than oral minoxidil with similar effectiveness, because it avoids first-pass liver metabolism [1]. Pharmacokinetic work on the product is ongoing [1].

Common effects of oral minoxidil include low blood pressure, fluid and salt retention, edema, rapid heartbeat, dizziness, headaches, excess hair growth and temporary shedding [1]. Pericardial and pleural effusion, tamponade and pseudoacromegaly are rare and linked to larger doses; cardiovascular complications are much less common at low hair-loss doses [1]. Contraindications include pheochromocytoma and prior pericarditis or pericardial effusion [1].

A preliminary trial of low-dose sublingual minoxidil reported no adverse effects or blood pressure changes, and a phase 3 sublingual minoxidil program from Samson Clinical was listed as of September 2025 [1]. Results from the phase 3 program were not available in the source consulted.

timeline.event: FDA approves oral minoxidil for hypertension [1].
Topical minoxidil (Rogaine) approved for male baldness [1].
Low-dose oral minoxidil for hair loss emerges [1].
Sublingual minoxidil listed in phase 3 trials [1].
